newsitem.title: UK: Five to contest leadership of UK Conservatives.
newsitem.headline: Five to contest leadership of UK Conservatives.

text.p: Nominations for candidates to lead Britain's crushed Conservative party closed on Thursday with former finance minister Kenneth Clarke the favourite of the five taking part.
Former prime minister John Major set the race in motion when he announced he was stepping down as party leader in the wake of the Conservatives' heavy election defeat by Labour on May 1.

The party's 164 members of parliament -- the only people entitled to cast ballots for a new party leader -- look set to give the pro-European Clarke the most votes in next Tuesday's first-round ballot.

Clarke fought a rearguard battle against right-wingers trying to hijack European policy before the election and could face a backlash in the second round of voting when some of his right-wing challengers drop out.
Second favourite is former Welsh Secretary William Hague, 36, who leads former interior minister Michael Howard, former social security secretary Peter Lilley and former Welsh secretary John Redwood.
Archie Hamilton, the senior MP in charge of the election, said it would be preferable if some of the five dropped out to speed up proceedings.
"I've always taken the view...that the sooner we can get this over and done with, the better, because we do need a new leader to galvanise the party and get it organised," he told BBC radio.
On Wednesday former health secretary Stephen Dorrell abandoned his flagging campaign and gave his backing to Clarke. Both men are on the centre-left of the party.
The winner in the first ballot needs an overall majority of the Conservative members of parliament -- plus a lead of 15 percent over his nearest rival.

In the second round on June 17, the winner needs a straight majority. But if no one succeeds -- and an outright winner is still unlikely -- the top two candidates go through to a straight fight on June 19.
The arcane nature of the election makes the outcome extremely hard to forecast, with MPs often switching allegiances between one round of voting and the next.

Margaret Thatcher, who beat Edward Heath in 1975 and went on to become one of the most prominent British prime ministers of the 20th century, was never initially thought likely to win the party leadership
